title: Why Sierra de Salamanca tastes the way it does

lede.text: Unlike most wine areas of Castilla y León, these terraces sit on acid soils of slate and granite. That ground and a mild, damp Mediterranean microclimate give wines with mineral notes and a long life.

chapters.title: Terraces above the Alagón
paras: The area lies in the south of Salamanca province and covers 482.10 km2. The land is twisting, and the vines grow on bancales, terraces on the slopes above the Alagón river and its tributaries. The slopes are steeper to the northwest and gentler in the south.

Growers have looked for the best-facing slopes for centuries, and these are often the steepest. Those slopes give the vines good sun and better air. They also hold back erosion. The area is traditionally called Sierra de Francia, because most of its villages sit on the foothills of that range.

fly.label: Sierra de Francia
fly.caption: The range on whose foothills most of the area's villages sit, on the banks of the Alagón.

chapters.title: Wet springs, dry harvests
paras: The climate is Mediterranean, with fairly short winters that are not very cold and long, hot, dry summers. Rain is plentiful in autumn and spring, and the yearly total tops 1,000 mm. That makes up for soils that hold little water.

Little rain falls in summer or at harvest, so fungal disease stays away and the grapes come in healthy. They are picked with high tartaric acid (over 7 g/l) and high sugar (a potential alcohol of 14.5º). Sun on the terraces and cold summer nights bring this about, helped by traditional growing and very old, well-adapted vines. This gives the wines a great capacity to age.

chapters.title: Acid slate and granite
paras: The rock is metamorphic in the west and plutonic in the east. Among the metamorphic rocks, lightly altered greenish-grey clay slates stand out, attributed to the Cambrian. The soils are acid, unlike most wine areas of Castilla y León, and mostly sandy loam.
Slate and granite soils give different grapes. Grapes from slate tend to very mineral notes and a very marked structure. Grapes from granite usually give more length and softness on the palate.

chapters.title: Rufete and very old vines
paras: Rufete is the grape native to the area. It is well adapted to the acid soils and the climate. Its wines show notes of red fruit and spice. Scrub herbs join them, with elegant, spicy tannins. Tempranillo turns out very balsamic here, with spicy touches. Garnacha Tinta is led by tart wild strawberry and a lot of minerality. These three are the only red grapes allowed.

The vines are very old: half the plots are over 80 years old and many are centenarian. The traditional planting is 4,400 vines per hectare, 1.5 m by 1.5 m, and it is still kept. The crowding makes the vines compete, so crops are very low. The rules cap yields at 7,000 kg per hectare for red grapes and 9,000 kg for white.

Reds aged in barrel must reach at least 12.0% alcohol. All the wines share medium-high alcohol. Their tartaric acidity is high and balanced, and their longevity medium-high. Mineral notes and scrub herbs such as fennel and thyme are common aromas.

fly.label: San Esteban de la Sierra
fly.caption: Through the refit of the cooperative here, the area began to revive.

terms.text: The name of one of the area's municipalities can go on the label with the words Vino de Pueblo, if the wine is made with 85% grapes from plots in that municipality.
